analysis.one_liner: Taxes private equity managers' performance fees as ordinary income instead of capital gains.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, was never taken up by the Ways and Means Committee, and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers are typically paid with a share of their fund's profits, and today most of that pay is taxed at the lower long-term capital-gains rate instead of the higher rates that apply to a salary. This bill would rework the rules so that a large slice of that performance pay is taxed as ordinary income, closing what critics call the carried interest loophole. It contains a formula that lets genuinely invested capital keep capital-gains treatment above a threshold return, so it aims at the service-fee slice, not at ordinary investment gains. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, whose fund managers currently pay a lower rate on their main source of income than salaried workers pay on wages; the change would also raise revenue that could reduce deficits or fund other priorities.

how_it_helps.text: Requires certain income from partnership interests held in connection with performing services to be treated as ordinary income rather than as capital gains.

Under the bill, the amount treated as ordinary income is capped by a formula tied to the fund's invested capital and a threshold return (the federal long-term rate plus 10 percentage points), so gains above that return on a manager's own money can still be capital gains.
It closes related workarounds, treating gains on distributions of property and transfers to related people as ordinary income as well.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers, whose main income would be taxed at ordinary-income rates of up to 37% instead of the 20% capital-gains rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: The recharacterization formula is highly complex, tracking invested capital, partner contributions, related-party loans, and threshold returns, which would create real compliance costs and likely require extensive regulations.

The bill applies broadly to any business of 'raising or returning capital' and 'investing in' or 'developing' trades or businesses, including research and experimentation activities, so it would reach beyond large buyout funds into venture capital and startup investing.
It took effect only for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, and applied prospectively, so it raised no revenue for years already past.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward fairness: managers' performance pay is compensation for services, and it would be taxed like other compensation. The tradeoff is complexity — the formula needed to separate service compensation from genuine investment returns is intricate and would demand careful IRS rulemaking. The design is more targeted than a blanket repeal, which lowers the risk of catching ordinary investors, but adds administrative burden for funds of all sizes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Grothman introduced the bill on June 15, 2021, as the sole sponsor.
It drew zero cosponsors from either party.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; that referral was the only committee action in the bill's entire history.
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the Congress expired on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers, who kept paying the lower capital-gains rate on their performance income, while wage earners saw no offsetting revenue or fairness change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.role: Sole sponsor, House Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put forward a formula that taxes fund managers' performance pay as ordinary income while sparing genuine investment gains.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Richard Neal)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral on the day of introduction.

against.name: American Investment Council (private equity trade association)
against.role: Industry lobby for private equity and credit firms
against.what_they_did: The private equity industry has long lobbied to preserve the carried interest capital-gains rate, and no member of either party cosponsored this repeal.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsor was a Republican and it drew no cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken to reveal where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their main income — a share of fund profits for managing other people's money — is currently taxed at the 20% capital-gains rate, far below the rates on a worker's salary. The bill would tax the service-driven slice of that pay as ordinary income, which is why the industry defends the existing rules.

industries.industry: Venture capital and startup investment funds
industries.note: The bill's definition covers businesses that raise capital, invest in and develop companies, and treats research and experimentation activities as within scope, so some venture fund carry would be recharacterized as ordinary income. Gains above the threshold return on a partner's actual capital would still get capital-gains treatment.
